prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms enabled frequency standards at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B046 as my single prize part, unchanged from round 1, and the exchange has made the case firmer rather than merely more popular. The chair's first question, whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes leave room, is answered by the physics. The comb (2005) is the ruler that counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. Neither contains the magic-wavelength condition, which cancels the light shift on the clock transition while holding a very large number of neutral atoms in a Lamb-Dicke lattice, and that is what changes stability by orders of magnitude through parallel interrogation. It is a different oscillator, not a better comb or a better ion trap. On timing, I see no reason to wait for the redefinition of the second: independent clocks in several countries and species agree at the 1e-18 level now, and that agreement is a stronger test than any metrological decision, which follows from the achievement. On credit, a two-name prize is defensible because the contributions are separable and decisive: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and built the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group took the platform to record systematic uncertainty and stability and developed the many-body clock physics. The citation should say 'invention and realization' and name magic-wavelength trapping, so that it reads as a prize for this invention and not for optical clocks in general. I would not widen it to Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto or others, since three names would dilute a clean origin story and still not settle priority.
statement.case_against: The reservations remain real and I do not think they are fully dissolved. A reader can still see the lattice clock as the third prize in one precision-spectroscopy lineage, and that is a judgement about prize philosophy, which Mehlig and Danielsson frame fairly when they weigh a new organising concept above a record-setting instrument. Pearce is right that Ye's contribution was a long accuracy programme more than a separate invention, so the 'co-invention' wording is only defensible if the citation says 'realization' explicitly. Early strontium and ytterbium lattice contributions by others are left outside two names, and I cannot settle those priority questions from the supplied record. Finally, I am not an expert on clock systematics, and I am relying on recollection of the achieved uncertainties, so my confidence in B046 comes from the independence of the confirmations and from my colleagues' expertise in this area more than from my own judgement of the systematics.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B038 first as a concept-level Z2 classification, mature and confirmed in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi2Se3, and says he would weigh a new organising idea above a record-setting instrument when the instrument's lineage was recently honoured.
responses.response: I accept that B038 is the deeper concept and I would not call a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize a mistake, which is why it is my first alternative. Where I part from you is on whether the clock is only an instrument. The magic-wavelength lattice is a new way of preparing a many-atom quantum system so that its internal transition is protected from its motion, and it has produced new physics of its own: many-body clock physics, relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, and constraints on varying constants. On B038 you concede that the credit chain is incomplete, and I think that matters more than the prize-philosophy question. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp observed, and the committee would be publishing a story with a visible gap in the middle. A citation limited to prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation lessens this but does not remove it, while B046 has no comparable gap among its credited names.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B038 from inflation, calls the lattice clock a very fine instrument and a refinement of precision timekeeping already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and a better way of making one measurement rather than a new observation about nature.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-engineering distinction seriously, but I think it misdescribes this case. The clock does not only make one measurement better. Comparing clocks at 1e-18 turns the instrument into an experiment about nature: gravitational redshift is resolved across millimetres to centimetres of height, and clock comparisons now bound variation of fundamental constants and certain dark-sector couplings. That is observation of nature enabled by a new quantum system, and it follows the same logic as past prizes for measurement inventions that opened new physics. I agree with you that the HgTe proposal is the real obstacle for B038, and I agree with your wording of a citation around prediction and first observation, but that wording leaves the gap in the story rather than closing it. I also hear that your own ranking rests partly on the cross-member support for B038, and I would treat support counts as no argument either way, including for B046.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B046 on atomic-structure grounds (polarizabilities, blackbody shifts) and asks whether Ye's role is the leading realisation and the systematic-uncertainty record rather than co-invention, and whether the prize should wait for the redefinition.
responses.response: I agree with your description of Ye's role and I think the citation should carry it: 'invention and realization' with magic-wavelength trapping named explicitly. My answer to the chair's second question is the same as yours. The achievement is already complete and verified by clock-to-clock comparison, and a Nobel decision should not depend on the schedule of a metrological body. Your atomic-structure point also supports the distinction from the 2005 prize, because the blackbody-shift and polarizability control that makes a magic wavelength usable is the content of the lattice clock and is not part of the comb. I would add one qualification to my own earlier position: I do not think the Ye role question can be settled by the supplied record any better than the Lemonde and Ludlow question, so I would keep the two-name configuration but state the division of labour in the citation.

responses.point: Olsson moved B046 to the head of her configuration, would keep Katori and Ye with a citation that names the magic-wavelength invention, and says the committee should not simply rotate toward the community of the 2025 circuit-physics prize.
responses.response: I agree with the citation wording and with keeping Katori and Ye. On your rotation concern, I think it is fair and it is a point on which I should be transparent: it is one of the reasons I stay with B046 and not with circuit QED. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, and a circuit-QED prize one year later would cluster the awards in a single community, which I am too close to judge. I do differ from you slightly on B006 as an alternative. You note that the committee should credit the original idea and demonstration rather than the engineering that followed, and I agree, but the original idea and demonstration (the 2004 proposal and the first strong-coupling experiments) are the core of B006, so it is not an engineering prize. The real obstacle is that the three-name limit forces an exclusion among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff, and I cannot argue that case neutrally. I list it as my second alternative for that reason and not because I consider it weaker.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B046 first, would not widen the prize beyond two names, and raised the question whether recusal regarding Ye should follow from his stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, which is near JILA.
responses.response: I agree with not widening the prize, for the reason that the magic-wavelength concept and the record-performance realisation are separable contributions with clear owners. On recusal, I think the chair's question about whether either of us should be weighted differently is answered by looking at the documented facts: your record shows a research stay in Hall's laboratory and no collaboration or relationship with Ye or Katori, so I read it as field proximity and not as a conflict that should reduce the weight of your position. My own position is different in kind, because my connection is to the circuit-QED candidate I now do not advocate, and I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye. If anything, my move from sixth to first for B046 is a point in its favour that is independent of any interest of mine.

uncertainties: Whether the committee finds that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems leave room for a prize on the magic-wavelength lattice clock; I judge that they do, but I cannot rule out that colleagues weigh the lineage differently.

Whether Katori and Ye are better credited as co-inventors or as inventor and realizer, and whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Schmidt or the Paris and PTB groups make a two-name prize unfair; I cannot settle priority from the supplied record.

Whether B038 can be given a defensible three-name configuration without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, since a prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would be my first alternative if the clock case is rejected.
For B006, which of Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff belong in a three-name credit, and how much a circuit-QED prize would cluster with the 2025 award in the same community.
I am recalling achieved clock uncertainties and early strontium history from memory and have not verified the current record values from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My documented connection is to circuit and waveguide QED: I work in this area at Chalmers, direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, have Chalmers colleagues (Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and a frequent co-author (Anton Frisk Kockum) in the field, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. This applies to B006, which I ranked first in my opening ballot and no longer advocate. If B006 became a leading candidate in the final decision I would recuse myself from it. I see no specific connection to Katori, Ye or B046, nor to B038, B042 or the other shortlisted candidates, and my move to B046 is not driven by any interest of mine. Eva Olsson is a Chalmers colleague, which is a general institutional link that is not tied to any candidate.
